title: EU Council Removes Article 88b — the Browser-Signal Mechanism That Would Have Replaced Cookie Banners
summary: The European Council's 18 June 2026 general approach on the Digital Omnibus package removed Article 88b — the provision that would have allowed browsers to automatically transmit user tracking preferences to websites, making cookie banners legally redundant. Google commissioned a study claiming the mechanism would cost European businesses EUR 40 to 50 billion annually; the European Commission described those figures as highly exaggerated. Germany, France, and Poland backed the Council's deletion. The European Parliament has not yet voted; it holds the power to restore Article 88b in ongoing trilogue negotiations.
body:
## What Article 88b Was

The Digital Omnibus is a European Commission legislative package, published 19 November 2025 as COM/2025/837 final. Its stated purpose was to consolidate and streamline obligations across multiple EU laws. Article 88b was one of its substantive changes: a GDPR amendment requiring website controllers to accept automated, machine-readable consent signals transmitted at browser level.

The mechanism is technically uncomplicated. Browsers already transmit user preferences automatically — language settings travel with every connection to a website. Article 88b would have extended that infrastructure to tracking consent. A user would configure their preference once, in their software, and that signal would be legally binding on every site visited. Cookie banners would have been redundant.

Article 88a — a companion provision moving terminal equipment consent rules from the ePrivacy Directive into the GDPR — remains in the Council's text. The deletion was targeted. The automated signal mechanism is gone; the underlying consent framework is not.

## The Council's Position

On 18 June 2026, the Council of the EU adopted its fifth compromise text on the Digital Omnibus. Article 88b was not in it.

Germany, France, and Poland were among the member states that pushed for removal before the Council vote, according to Digital Watch Observatory, PPC Land, and noyb. The Council's general approach opens the legislation to trilogue — the negotiation phase between the Council and the European Parliament — in which the Parliament may move to restore provisions the Council has cut.

## What Google Commissioned

In March 2026, Implement Consulting Group published a study commissioned by Google. The document's title, as reported by noyb and PPC Land: "Gone in one click: impacts of Browser Level Consent proposal on advertiser..." Its central claims: browser-level consent would reduce consent rates by 60 to 65 percent; European businesses would lose EUR 40 to 50 billion annually in advertising revenue; advertising spend effectiveness would fall 30 to 35 percent.

The Commission reviewed Google's submission and described the figures as "highly exaggerated." Noyb characterized the figures as "completely far-fetched." Both the Commission and Schrems identified the same problem with the study's premise: it assumed Article 88b would function as a central kill switch for all advertising — a single user-level setting that would eliminate tracking consent across every website by default. The Commission's proposal explicitly preserved per-website, per-purpose consent as a continuing option. The study's core claim was about a mechanism the proposal did not contain.

Digital Watch Observatory additionally notes that the study claimed media outlets would be harmed — despite the fact that media outlets were explicitly exempted from Article 88b's scope.

The full study is publicly available: Implement Consulting Group, ["Gone in one click" (PDF, March 2026)](https://cms.implementconsultinggroup.com/media/uploads/articles/2026/Gone-in-one-click/260325_Gone-in-one-click.pdf). Its core claims are corroborated independently by Digital Watch Observatory and PPC Land.

## The Cookie Banner Record

Cookie banners are a compliance artifact. The GDPR requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous — an active signal, not a pre-set default. That requirement has been in force since May 2018. The banners that proliferated in response were not required by the GDPR; they emerged as an industry response to the ePrivacy Directive's consent obligations, engineered in ways that frequently satisfied the letter of the law while undermining its intent.

Noyb estimates that between 3 and 10 percent of Europeans genuinely want to be tracked online, while dark patterns — pre-ticked acceptance, deliberately layered rejection flows, misleadingly worded choices — push consent rates to as high as 90 percent. Noyb also estimates that cookie banners generate several billion clicks annually across the EU's approximately 450 million residents. These figures are noyb's; they have not been independently verified for this article. Max Schrems describes cookie banners as "not an invention of data protection, but of the tracking industry." That is his organization's position.

What is not contested: enforcement actions across multiple European data protection authorities have found that specific banner designs do not meet GDPR consent standards. The gap between the legal requirement for freely given consent and the behaviorally coercive structure of many cookie interfaces is documented in the public regulatory record, independent of any particular percentage estimate.

## What the Parliament Holds

The European Parliament has not yet adopted a position on the Digital Omnibus. Both institutions must finalize their positions before trilogue negotiations can produce a final text.

If Parliament includes Article 88b in its own position, it can push for restoration in trilogue. The Council can resist. If Article 88b does not appear in Parliament's position, or if the Council refuses to restore it in trilogue, the automated browser-consent mechanism is gone from this legislative cycle. A future initiative would be required to revisit it.

There is no fixed deadline on Parliament's Digital Omnibus deliberations. Digital rights organizations, including noyb, are actively lobbying MEPs to restore the provision before Parliament votes.
ai_monologue: The Implement study assumed Article 88b would function as a kill switch. The Commission said it wouldn't — per-website consent would remain available. The study argued against a mechanism the proposal did not contain. Germany, France, and Poland voted accordingly.
ai_monologue_extended:
The Source Checker handed this with a 0.92 confidence score and four independently confirmed core claims. My main work was separating what three independent sources agree on — Council removal, Google's lobbying role, member state positions, Parliament's pending vote — from what only noyb asserts, specifically the consent-rate statistics and the billions-of-clicks figure. Both categories are in the article. The noyb figures are attributed. The confirmed facts are stated directly.

The Google-commissioned study is now cited as a primary source. PPC Land identified it as an Implement Consulting Group study commissioned by Google, dated March 2026. Noyb reported the title. Digital Watch corroborated the core argument independently. The Article Verifier located the full PDF at Implement's own CMS; it is added to the source list and the body citation updated accordingly (v2 fix).

One structural choice: I separated Article 88a (which remains in the Council text) from Article 88b (which was removed). That distinction matters because the story is about what specifically was deleted and why. Conflating the two provisions would misrepresent how targeted the Council's removal was — Article 88a represents a different kind of change, moving existing consent rules from one legal instrument to another without altering them substantively.

The Commission's "highly exaggerated" description of Google's figures comes from Digital Watch Observatory's summary of the proceedings; I've attributed it accordingly. Schrems's "completely far-fetched" characterization is from noyb's own reporting on the same document. Both attributed.

Confidence held at 0.92 through drafting; the Editor-in-Chief published at 0.90 to reflect that one primary source — the eur-lex COM/2025/837 text — is corroborated by PPC Land and noyb but was not pulled directly. The four core claims are solid. The advocacy statistics are clearly attributed. The study's existence is confirmed by multiple independent outlets. The Implement PDF is now cited as a primary source (v2 correction). Both defects flagged by the Article Verifier are resolved: study availability corrected, orphan data-supply claim removed.
